extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and advanced undergraduates studying set theory/forcing (readers of Evan Chen's Napkin notes)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, lemmas, and constructions for building generic extensions by forcing (names, forcing relation, poset properties) and using them to add many reals so as to violate the Continuum Hypothesis. Focused on the poset Add(ω,ω2), chain conditions, and preservation of cardinals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dense subset
rubrics_metrics.description: A subset D ⊆ P is dense if for all p ∈ P, there exists a q ∈ D such that q ≤ p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the entire P and any downward slice. In the infinite binary tree, D = {all strings ending in 001} is dense. In (N, ≥) a set is dense iff it has infinitely many elements (e.g., evens or primes). Being dense is central to the definition of M-generic (must meet every dense set in M).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility / Incompatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: For p, q ∈ P write p ∥ q if there exists r ∈ P with r ≤ p and r ≤ q; otherwise p ⊥ q (incompatible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the infinite binary tree no two elements are compatible unless comparable. Compatibility determines whether two conditions can simultaneously be extended in a filter; used in definitions of filters and antichains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter on a poset
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonempty set G ⊆ P is a filter if (a) G is upwards-closed: ∀p ∈ G(∀q ≥ p)(q ∈ G), and (b) any pair of elements in G is compatible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: if G is a filter then 1_P ∈ G. Filters are the basic objects which, when M-generic, give rise to extensions M[G].

rubrics_metrics.name: M-generic filter
rubrics_metrics.description: G is M-generic if for all D which are in the model M, if D is dense then G ∩ D ≠ ∅.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The requirement D ∈ M is essential: there can be dense sets not in M that avoid a given filter. Examples: generic filters on 2^{<ω} correspond to infinite binary sequences that 'contain every finite string'; if G ∈ M it cannot be M-generic (there are dense sets in M missing it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rasiowa–Sikorski lemma (existence of generic filters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose M is a countable transitive model of ZFC and P is a partial order. Then there exists an M-generic filter G.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: 'hit them one by one' — enumerate the dense sets in M and choose conditions meeting them inductively. This lemma justifies existence of generic filters for countable M.

rubrics_metrics.name: Splitting poset
rubrics_metrics.description: A partial order P is splitting if for all p ∈ P, there exists q, r ≤ p such that q ⊥ r.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the infinite binary tree is (very) splitting (take two immediate successors). Splitting is used to guarantee that a generic set G is not in M: see Lemma 93.2.5 (Splitting posets omit generic sets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Splitting posets omit generic sets (Lemma 93.2.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If P is splitting, then if F ⊆ P is a filter such that F ∈ M, then P \ F is dense. In particular, if G ⊆ P is generic, then G ∉ M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: for any p∈F, splitting provides q,r ≤ p with q ⊥ r; F cannot contain both, so some q ≤ p is outside F, showing P\F is dense. This ensures generic filters cannot already lie in M.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of P-names and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Define Name_0 = ∅, Name_{α+1} = P(Name_α × P), Name_λ = ⋃_{α<λ} Name_α, and Name = ⋃_α Name_α. For a filter G, interpret τ^G = {σ^G | ⟨σ, p⟩ ∈ τ and p ∈ G}. Then M[G] = {τ^G | τ ∈ Name^M}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of P-names as 'fuzzy sets' whose realizations depend on G. Examples: ˇx = {⟨ˇy,1_P⟩ | y ∈ x} satisfies (ˇx)^G = x; ˙P := {⟨ˇp,p⟩ | p ∈ P} satisfies (˙P)^G = G. M[G] is transitive and extends M.

rubrics_metrics.name: M[G] satisfies basic ZF axioms from a filter (Lemma 93.3.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If G is a filter and M a transitive model of ZFC, then M[G] is transitive and satisfies Extensionality, Foundation, EmptySet, Infinity, Pairing, and Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch: ˇx names embed M into M[G]; pairing and union are constructed via simple names. Remaining axioms (PowerSet, Replacement, Choice) require the forcing theorem machinery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forcing relation (informal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Roughly, p ⊩ φ(σ1,...,σn) (p forces the formula φ with names σ_i) iff for any M-generic G with p ∈ G, M[G] ⊨ φ[σ1^G,...,σn^G].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key point: ⊩ is definable in M and does not reference a particular G. The Fundamental Theorem ties forcing in M to truth in M[G].

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental theorem of forcing (Theorem 93.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose M is a transitive model of ZF, P ∈ M a poset, and G ⊆ P is M-generic. For σ1,...,σn ∈ Name^M, M[G] ⊨ φ[σ1^G,...,σn^G] iff there exists p ∈ G with p ⊩ φ(σ1,...,σn). Moreover, the forcing relation is uniformly definable in M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central bridge allowing one to work inside M to decide what will be true in M[G].

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive definition of the forcing relation (Definition 93.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For p ∈ P and formula φ(σ1,...,σn) define p ⊩ ... by induction: (1) p ⊩ τ1 = τ2 iff for each ⟨σ1,q1⟩ ∈ τ1 a certain set D_{σ1,q1} is dense below p (encoding τ1 ⊆ τ2), and symmetrically for τ2; (2) p ⊩ τ1 ∈ τ2 iff the set {q | ∃⟨τ,r⟩∈τ2 (q≤r ∧ q ⊩ (τ=τ1))} is dense below p; (3) p ⊩ φ∧ψ iff p ⊩ φ and p ⊩ ψ; (4) p ⊩ ¬φ iff ∀q ≤ p, q ̸⊩ φ; (5) p ⊩ ∃xφ(x,...) iff {q | ∃τ (q ⊩ φ(τ,...))} is dense below p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Atomic cases require induction on ranks of names. The definition only refers to objects in M, hence is definable in M. This explicit form is used to prove consistency/persistence and the Fundamental Theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and Persistence (Lemma 93.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) (Consistency) If p ⊩ φ and q ≤ p then q ⊩ φ. (2) (Persistence) If {q | q ⊩ φ} is dense below p then p ⊩ φ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both are proved by induction on formula complexity. They imply completeness: {p | p ⊩ φ or p ⊩ ¬φ} is dense, so generics decide every statement by some condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness corollary
rubrics_metrics.description: The set {p | p ⊩ φ or p ⊩ ¬φ} is dense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence of Consistency and Persistence; ensures M-generic G will meet a condition that either forces φ or forces ¬φ, so M[G] has a definite truth value for φ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic extension satisfies ZFC (Theorem 93.6.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If M is a transitive model of ZFC, P ∈ M a poset, and G ⊆ P is M-generic, then M[G] ⊨ ZFC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch given for Comprehension: use Fundamental Theorem to describe the comprehension set A in M[G] and build a name τ ∈ Name^M with τ^G = A. Other axioms are handled similarly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poset Add(ω,ω2) to add many reals
rubrics_metrics.description: In M, define P = Add(ω,ω2) := ({p : ω2×ω → 2, dom(p) finite}, ⊇). Order: p ≤ q iff dom(p) ⊇ dom(q) and p,q agree on dom(q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A generic G can be encoded as a function ω2×ω → 2, and for each α ∈ ω2 define G_α = {n | G(α,n)=0} which yields ω2 many distinct reals in M[G]. Need to ensure no cardinal-collapse to make these truly ω2 many reals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong antichain
rubrics_metrics.description: A ⊆ P is a strong antichain if for any distinct p and q in A, we have p ⊥ q (they are incompatible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stronger than mere incomparability. In forcing literature some authors call this simply an 'antichain'. Example in binary tree: {00,01,10,11} is a strong antichain (maximal).

rubrics_metrics.name: κ-chain condition (κ-cc) and c.c.c.
rubrics_metrics.description: A poset P has the κ-chain condition if all strong antichains in P have size less than κ. The special case κ = ℵ1 is the countable chain condition (c.c.c.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If P has the κ-cc (in M) then P preserves cardinals ≥ κ (more precisely: chain conditions preserve regular cardinals ≥ κ). Used to avoid cardinal collapse when adding reals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible Values Argument (Lemma 94.2.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose M is a transitive model and P has the κ-chain condition in M. Let X,Y ∈ M and f:X→Y be in M[G] but f∉M. Then there exists F ∈ M with F:X→P(Y) such that for any x∈X, f(x)∈F(x) and |F(x)|_M < κ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Idea: each possible value of f(x) corresponds to some condition forcing that value; distinct values require incompatible conditions, so κ-cc bounds the number of possibilities. This lets M 'approximate' values of new functions by small sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserving cardinals and regular cardinals (Definition 94.3.1 & Prop 94.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: P preserves cardinals if for every M-generic G the models M and M[G] agree on the sentence 'κ is a cardinal' for every κ. Similarly for preserving regular cardinals. Moreover, preserving cardinals ⇔ preserving regular cardinals (in the appropriate ranges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces cardinal-preservation questions to preserving regularity, which is amenable to the Possible Values Argument and chain condition hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain conditions preserve regular cardinals (Theorem 94.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If M satisfies 'P has the κ-chain condition and κ is regular', then P preserves regularity greater than or equal to κ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: use the Possible Values Argument to show no new cofinal functions can collapse regularity. Thus, if P is c.c.c. it preserves all cardinals and cofinalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Δ-system lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: If C is an uncountable collection of finite sets then there exists an uncountable subcollection C' ⊆ C which is a Δ-system: there is a root R such that for any distinct X,Y in C', X ∩ Y = R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses pigeonhole on sizes and induction. Two cases: some element appears in uncountably many sets (remove it), or each element appears only countably often (build disjoint sets). The Δ-system lemma is a standard combinatorial tool used in proving c.c.c. for Add(ω,κ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Add(ω,κ) satisfies the countable chain condition (Lemma 94.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For all κ, Add(ω,κ) satisfies the countable chain condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch: assume an uncountable strong antichain {p_α | α<ω1}. Consider the collection of finite domains C = {dom(p_α)}; apply Δ-system lemma to get an uncountable Δ-system with root R. Among those with the same restriction to R there must be two identical functions, contradicting incompatibility. Thus no uncountable strong antichain exists.
